skill.name: marketing-psychology
skill.description: Apply psychological principles, mental models, and behavioral science to marketing strategy, messaging, pricing, conversion, and customer behavior analysis.
skill.summary: Apply behavioral science and mental models to ethical marketing decisions.
skill.author: coreyhaines31

finding_verdicts.reason: Line 41 explains the inversion mental model by asking what would cause failure and avoiding those factors. This is marketing strategy prose, not system reconnaissance or environment discovery.
Line 46 describes Occam's Razor and advises against overcomplicating strategy. It contains no request to inspect host systems, files, networks, or user environment details.
Line 91 explains the Barbell Strategy as a budgeting and risk-allocation model. The safety and risk wording is conceptual marketing guidance, not security probing.
Line 93 gives a marketing budget example for proven channels and experimental bets. It does not instruct collection of system information or execution of diagnostic commands.
Line 112 defines the availability heuristic in customer decision-making. It discusses human judgment and examples, with no technical reconnaissance behavior.
Line 202 defines regret aversion as a buyer psychology concept. The phrase about avoiding regret is not an instruction to probe or enumerate a system.
Line 250 describes the foot-in-the-door technique using a subscription upgrade path. The content is about customer commitment stages, not system reconnaissance.
Line 258 explains loss aversion and how people respond to potential losses. It contains no technical discovery, host inspection, or security bypass instruction.

content.value_statement: Marketing teams often struggle to explain why customers hesitate, buy, or churn. This skill maps those problems to proven mental models and ethical actions.
actual_capabilities: Maps marketing challenges to relevant psychological principles and mental models.
Explains the buyer behavior behind each recommended model.
Suggests ethical marketing applications for messaging, pricing, funnels, and retention.
Provides clarifying questions about audience beliefs, journey stage, and conversion blockers.
Offers quick references for trust, urgency, pricing, onboarding, and growth problems.
limitations: Does not run experiments or measure campaign performance directly.
Does not replace customer interviews, analytics, or market research.
Does not provide legal, compliance, or dark-pattern review.
Cannot guarantee that a psychological model will improve results.

use_cases.title: Improve conversion messaging
use_cases.description: Find the mental models that explain hesitation on a landing page, checkout flow, or email campaign.

use_cases.title: Shape ethical persuasion
use_cases.description: Use social proof, authority, urgency, and commitment principles without misleading customers.

use_cases.title: Diagnose pricing resistance
use_cases.description: Analyze objections using anchoring, framing, mental accounting, and loss aversion.

prompt_templates.title: Find useful models
prompt_templates.prompt: I am marketing [product] to [audience]. The main challenge is [challenge]. Which mental models should I consider first?

prompt_templates.title: Improve a message
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this marketing message using behavioral science. Explain which psychology principles apply and suggest ethical improvements: [paste copy].

prompt_templates.title: Diagnose funnel friction
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze this funnel stage for psychological friction. Audience: [audience]. Desired action: [action]. Current blocker: [blocker].

prompt_templates.title: Build a test plan
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a prioritized experiment plan using mental models. Include the hypothesis, target behavior, model used, ethical guardrails, and success metric.

output_examples.input: A SaaS trial page has many visits but few starts.
output_examples.output: The skill may identify activation energy, status-quo bias, and regret aversion. It may recommend reducing form fields, adding a no-commitment message, and showing a quick first win.

output_examples.input: A pricing page gets frequent objections that the product feels expensive.
output_examples.output: The skill may apply anchoring, mental accounting, and price relativity. It may suggest clearer tier contrast, daily cost framing, and stronger outcome-based value proof.

output_examples.input: A brand wants stronger trust in a new market.
output_examples.output: The skill may recommend authority bias, social proof, and mere exposure. It may suggest expert endorsements, customer examples, and consistent repeated touchpoints.

best_practices: Start with the exact customer behavior you want to influence.
Use psychological principles to clarify value, not to hide tradeoffs.
Test recommendations with real audience data before scaling them.
anti_patterns: Using scarcity, urgency, or social proof when the claim is not true.
Applying every mental model at once instead of choosing the most relevant few.
Treating psychology frameworks as proof without customer evidence.

faq.question: What does this skill help with?
faq.answer: It helps connect marketing problems to psychology principles, mental models, and ethical persuasion tactics.

faq.question: Can it write marketing copy?
faq.answer: It can suggest copy improvements and explain the psychology behind them. It is strongest when paired with specific audience context.

faq.question: Does it support pricing strategy?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers anchoring, framing, mental accounting, tier design, and discount perception.

faq.question: Is this only for conversion optimization?
faq.answer: No. It also supports positioning, trust building, onboarding, retention, growth loops, and campaign planning.

faq.question: How should I use it responsibly?
faq.answer: Use it to reduce confusion and match customer needs. Avoid false urgency, hidden costs, or misleading proof.

faq.question: Which AI tools can use it?
faq.answer: The report lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.
